identity_notes: Blueberry's retrieval set is dominated by a large false-match cluster around 'blueberry muffin baby/rash/sign', a well-established dermatological/hematological term for congenital dermal erythropoiesis (seen in TORCH infections, neonatal leukemia, neuroblastoma, Gaucher disease, histiocytosis, etc.) that has nothing to do with blueberry food or supplementation -- all rejected off_topic (~15 case reports). A second cluster is agricultural/horticultural and food-science research on blueberry cultivation, ripening, packaging, and meat/shrimp preservation, also off_topic. Among genuine human intervention trials, blueberry has an unusually large and consistent evidence base for cognitive function (children, healthy adults, older adults, and mild cognitive impairment -- both acute and chronic dosing), vascular/endothelial function (flow-mediated dilation is the most consistently positive endpoint per meta-analyses 38887319/41974068), and cardiometabolic/type 2 diabetes parameters, generally with more consistent positive signals for vascular and cognitive endpoints than for hard blood-pressure or lipid endpoints. A recurring nuance is plant part and preparation: most trials use whole/freeze-dried fruit, juice, or standardized anthocyanin extract (all flagged exact_match), but a minority use blueberry LEAVES (as tea or leaf extract; 31941864, 40195645) or a different Vaccinium species (V. meridionale/agraz, 40772130) -- these are flagged related_form_differs since they represent a different plant part or species from the fruit typically meant by 'blueberry' on a supplement label. Many kept records combine blueberry with cranberry, grape, banana, soluble fiber, creatine/leucine blends, or other natural products, also flagged related_form_differs where blueberry's isolated contribution cannot be determined. A 2019 systematic review on blueberry and cognition (30941401) was subsequently subject to published methodological critique regarding effect-size calculation errors (32090247, 32658969, both rejected as correspondence rather than primary data) -- reviewers should weight 30941401's conclusions with this caveat in mind.
